DOCUMENT:
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place." -- Table 1 shows mushroom risotto has the highest gross margin on the menu (80%); the weakest is sirloin steak (60%). Lowest sales is correct (90 plates, tied with specials), but the margin claim misreads the table.
2. [missing_consideration] at: "The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target." -- The projection uses current food costs, but section 4 states beef prices rise 12% from 1 April, the same date as the new prices. Burgers and steaks (380 plates a week) would see higher food costs (e.g. about £1.25 more per steak), eroding much of the projected gain; the margin and profit projections never account for it.
3. [inconsistency] at: "keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week" -- Section 2 says the restaurant is open Wednesday to Sunday, i.e. five days a week; the recommendation refers to six trading days.

REVIEW:
# Review: Menu Pricing Review, Spring 2026

The price increases themselves look reasonable, and most of the arithmetic checks out. But the risotto proposal is based on a misreading of Table 1: the dish has the **best** margin on the menu, not the worst. The profit projection also leaves out the beef price rise flagged in section 4. Both points change the conclusions.

## 1. The risotto has the strongest margin, not the weakest

Table 1 shows the mushroom risotto at **80%**, the highest gross margin of any dish. Section 5.2 and your summary both say it is the weakest.

In cash terms it's also among the better dishes:

| Dish | Gross profit per plate |
|---|---|
| Sirloin steak | £15.60 |
| Fish and chips | £11.40 |
| **Mushroom risotto** | **£11.20** |
| Chicken curry | £10.90 |
| Beef burger | £10.80 |

Its only weakness is volume, at 90 plates a week, which ties with specials for the lowest.

**Replacing it could cost money.** Your specials run at **64%**. A replacement at the same £14.00 price and that margin would earn about £8.96 a plate rather than £11.20. On 90 plates that is about **£200 a week, or £10,500 a year, less**.

It is also currently your **only fixed vegetarian main**, so removing it carries a risk to bookings that the paper doesn't consider.

**Options:** keep the risotto, or replace it only with a vegetarian dish costed to at least an 80% margin. If low volume is the concern, try promoting it before cutting it.

## 2. The projection ignores the beef price rise

Section 4 says beef rises **12% from 1 April**, the same day the new prices take effect. Section 5.3 treats food costs as unchanged.

If the whole plate cost were beef, which is an upper bound, the increase would be:
- **Burger:** £4.20 × 12% ≈ £0.50 a plate × 260 = about **£131 a week**
- **Steak:** £10.40 × 12% ≈ £1.25 a plate × 120 = about **£150 a week**

That is up to **about £280 a week** (about £14,600 a year) eaten by higher costs. The true figure will be somewhat lower, since chips and garnish aren't beef, but it will be material. Get the beef share of each plate cost from the kitchen and use that figure.

**The steak in particular:** a £2.00 rise against up to £1.25 of extra cost leaves a margin of about **58%**, *below* today's 60%. The price increase barely keeps pace with costs.

## 3. Corrected effect, roughly

| Item | Weekly |
|---|---|
| Price increases (paper's figure, which checks out) | +£810 |
| Beef cost rise (upper bound) | up to −£280 |
| Risotto replaced with a 64% special | about −£200 |
| **Net** | **about +£330 a week, or about £17,000 a year** |

That compares with the claimed **£42,000**. Even keeping the risotto, the figure is about **£27,500**, before allowing for any loss of volume.

## 4. The 71% margin figure

I can reproduce "about 71%" only by **excluding specials** (whose price isn't given) and **ignoring the beef increase**. With the beef rise included, main-course margin comes out at roughly **69.5–70%**. That is still an improvement, but smaller than stated. The paper should show this calculation.

## 5. "Volumes will hold" is assumed, not tested

The paper offers no evidence beyond loyalty and the fact that the 2024 increase "had no visible effect." Two useful additions:
- **A break-even volume for each dish.** For example, fish and chips can lose about 25 plates a week (8%) at the new price before gross profit falls below today's level. That gives the owners a concrete threshold to watch for.
- **Quantify weekday lunch.** "A small share" should be a number, since it's the price-sensitive part of the trade.

## 6. Monitoring

- **Baseline:** January–February is the quietest season of the year, so April–May volumes will likely be higher regardless (Easter, better weather). The comparison could hide genuine losses. Compare with April–May 2025 instead, if you have it.
- **No action threshold.** Set one in advance, for example "if any repriced dish falls more than 10% against last spring for three consecutive weeks, review."

## 7. Smaller points

- **Trading days:** section 2 says Wednesday to Sunday, which is **five** days. Section 8 says "six trading days a week."
- **Competitor midpoints:** all three new prices are below the midpoint, as claimed (£17.98, £16.50 and £29.50). ✓
- **Arithmetic:** dish margins, plate totals (1,050) and the £810 / £42,120 calculation are all correct. ✓
- **Loyalty:** the 60% repeat rate cuts both ways, since regulars are the guests most likely to notice a price rise.

## Your summary against the document

| Claim | Status |
|---|---|
| Below competitor midpoints | ✓ |
| £810/week, £42,000/year | Before the beef rise and the risotto swap. Realistically about £17,000–£27,500 |
| Margin lifts to about 71% | About 69.5–70% after beef costs |
| Risotto has the weakest margin | ✗ Highest margin (80%) |
| Eight-week monitoring is an early warning | Needs a like-for-like baseline and thresholds |

## Suggested revisions

1. Withdraw or rethink the risotto removal, and keep a vegetarian main at a strong margin.
2. Include the beef increase, using the beef share of each plate cost, and restate the gross profit and margin.
3. Consider a slightly larger steak increase if the 60% margin matters.
4. Add break-even volumes for each dish and size the weekday lunch trade.
5. Use last spring as the monitoring baseline and set action thresholds.
6. Change "six trading days" to "five".

The price rises are well judged against competitors and probably worth doing. The paper just needs to show their true net value and drop the risotto cut.
